displayQuote: Every joke is a tiny revolution

meta.title: Who really said "Every joke is a tiny revolution"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Orwell really wrote it. The line is from his essay Funny, But Not Vulgar, first published in Leader magazine, London, on 28 July 1945.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Every joke is a tiny revolution'?
meta.ogDescription: Verified: George Orwell, Funny, But Not Vulgar, Leader magazine, 28 July 1945. Not a slogan — the second half of his definition of humour.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This one is real. The sentence appears in Orwell’s essay Funny, But Not Vulgar, first published in Leader magazine, London, on 28 July 1945, and reprinted in volume 3 of his Collected Essays, Journalism and Letters. Quote Investigator ↗ concludes the credit belongs to Orwell for what he wrote in 1945.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: The Collected Essays, Journalism and Letters, vol. 3: As I Please 1943–1946

source.excerpt: A thing is funny when — in some way that is not actually offensive or frightening — it upsets the established order. Every joke is a tiny revolution.
trail: The wording checks out against the essay: the full text at the orwell.ru library ↗ carries the sentence in its original paragraph, under a header giving first publication as Leader, London, 28 July 1945.
The specialists have already ruled. Quote Investigator’s investigation of this exact line ↗ concludes that George Orwell should receive credit for what he wrote in 1945.

For a page reference, QI cites the reprint in George Orwell: The Collected Essays, Journalism and Letters, volume 3, As I Please 1943–1946, edited by Sonia Orwell and Ian Angus (Nonpareil / David R. Godine) — essay starting at page 283, the sentence on page 284.
An independent citation record at WIST Quotations ↗ gives the same essay, the same 28 July 1945 Leader publication, and notes the piece was written in December 1944.
source.excerptNote: The sentence that follows in the essay offers a one-phrase definition of humour built on the image of dignity meeting a tin-tack; the sentence before it concedes that we do not know how laughter originated. Orwell’s claim is about what causes laughter, and the “tiny revolution” is his summary of that cause.

author.name: George Orwell
author.heading: Who was George Orwell?
author.bio: Born Eric Arthur Blair in Motihari, British India, in 1903, Orwell built his reputation as much on essays and reportage as on the two novels everyone remembers. Funny, But Not Vulgar belongs to the run of short critical pieces he wrote for the London press in the mid-1940s, in which he treated popular culture — comic postcards, boys’ weeklies, murder trials, jokes — as serious political evidence. He died in London in January 1950.

misattribution.heading: The attribution is right — the quotation isn’t always
misattribution.intro: This is one of the rare Orwell lines that survives checking. What does not survive is the way it travels: the wording mutates, the other half of the thought gets dropped, and for a while a Czechoslovak joke-collector was credited with it instead.

items.why: Kalina was a professor at the Czech Film and Theatre School who collected and circulated subversive jokes in the 1960s and 70s, and was imprisoned and then exiled for it. When ITV dramatised his story in 1981 under the title Tiny Revolutions, The Guardian’s review of 19 September 1981 credited the saying to Kalina, describing him as having called each of his jokes a tiny revolution. Quote Investigator, which transcribes that review line ↗, notes that Orwell’s use came first in 1945 and says it does not know whether Kalina’s coinage was independent.

Orwell wrote tiny. The little version is common enough that John Keane’s 12 May 2012 piece in The Conversation ↗ ran under the headline “Every Joke is a Little Revolution” while the body of the same article renders Orwell’s phrase as tiny revolution — the drift happening inside a single article.

Quoted alone the line reads as a blanket endorsement of joking. In the essay itself ↗ it follows directly from a conditional: a thing is funny when, in a way that is not actually offensive or frightening, it upsets the established order. Orwell is defining a mechanism, not issuing a manifesto — and in the same essay he argues that comedy without a serious purpose fails.

misattribution.truthLine: Orwell wrote it, in Funny, But Not Vulgar, first published in Leader magazine, London, on 28 July 1945 ↗; Quote Investigator ↗ concludes the credit belongs to him for what he wrote that year.

context.heading: Why he wrote it
lead: The line is not a standalone aphorism — it is a definition. Orwell was arguing that a thing is funny when it upsets the established order without being genuinely offensive or frightening; the revolution image is his gloss on that mechanism. He then complains that the English humorists of the day were too genteel, too kind-hearted and too consciously lowbrow ↗ to manage it, and that the best comic writers of the period succeeded precisely because they had a serious purpose and were willing to hit below the belt.

The timing matters. Orwell wrote the piece in December 1944 and it ran the following July, as the war in Europe ended — the moment when British comedy’s permitted targets were about to be renegotiated. According to WIST’s citation record ↗, the December 1944 composition date and the 28 July 1945 publication date are both attached to the essay.
context.detailsSummary: How the line reached the internet
detailsBody: Almost nobody quoting the line today is quoting Leader. The essay was rescued from the magazines in 1968, when Sonia Orwell and Ian Angus gathered Orwell’s uncollected journalism into the four-volume Collected Essays, Journalism and Letters; Quote Investigator cites the reprint in volume 3, As I Please 1943–1946, with the sentence falling on page 284 of an essay beginning at 283.

The Folio Society later titled a 1998 Orwell selection after the essay, and the Internet Archive holds a borrowable scan of it ↗. Which is the practical reason the quote circulates in isolation: it entered general use through anthologies and quote lists, not through the paragraph it was built for.
